questions.stem: The flash point of a fuel is the:
options: Temperature at which it boils in an open pan
Temperature at which it begins to freeze solid
Lowest temperature at which its vapour can briefly ignite
Temperature at which it burns with no ignition source nearby
questions.explanation: A low flash point means vapour can ignite at ordinary temperatures.

questions.stem: Diesel is preferred to gasoline aboard vessels mainly because diesel:
options: Burns without needing as much air
Costs less in every region of the coast
Has a higher flash point and less explosive vapour
Never needs filtering before the engine
questions.explanation: Higher flash point makes diesel much safer to store and handle on a vessel.

questions.stem: Oily rags left in a pile in a warm space are dangerous because they can:
options: Heat up and ignite on their own
Block the bilge pump suction
Attract rats and mice into the space
Corrode the deck plating below
questions.explanation: Oxidising oil generates heat that can lead to spontaneous combustion. Store rags in a closed metal container.

questions.stem: Which fire class involves flammable liquids such as fuel and oil?
options: Class C
Class B
Class D
Class A
questions.explanation: A is ordinary combustibles, B is flammable liquids and gases such as fuel and oil, C is live electrical equipment and D is combustible metals. Fuel and oil are Class B.

questions.stem: Fuel tank vent outlets are fitted with fine wire mesh mainly to:
options: Stop fuel overflowing
Keep dirt and insects out of the fuel
Stop flame entering the tank
Reduce fuel evaporation
questions.explanation: The mesh acts as a flame arrester.

questions.stem: The three sides of the fire triangle are:
options: Fuel, heat and oxygen
Heat, spark and gas
Oil, air and electricity
Fuel, smoke and water
questions.explanation: Remove any one side and the fire goes out. Cooling removes heat, smothering removes oxygen, and shutting a fuel valve removes fuel.

questions.stem: A fire in a live switchboard is classed as:
options: Class D
Class C
Class A
Class B
questions.explanation: Class C is live electrical equipment. Class A is ordinary combustibles, B is flammable liquids and gases, and D is combustible metals.

questions.stem: Why must you run the bilge blower before starting an inboard gasoline engine?
options: It dries the bilge and stops rust
It warms the fuel for easy starting
Gasoline vapour is lighter than air and floats to the deckhead
Gasoline vapour is heavier than air and pools in the bilge
questions.explanation: Gasoline and LPG vapour sink and pool low. Ventilating and checking by smell removes the explosive mixture before the starter sparks.

questions.stem: You find fuel dripping from a hose onto a hot exhaust manifold. The most appropriate first action is to:
options: Leave it until the end of the watch
Stop the engine and fix the leak after it cools
Wipe it with a rag and carry on running
Spray water on the hot manifold to cool it down
questions.explanation: Fuel on a hot surface is one of the commonest causes of engine-room fires. Stop the source, let the engine cool, repair, clean up, and log it. Water on a hot manifold can crack it.

questions.stem: Why must a space where batteries are charging be ventilated?
options: Charging gives off carbon monoxide only
The acid evaporates and clogs the vents
Charging gives off hydrogen, which is explosive
Batteries need cool moving air to hold their charge
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is released during charging and can form an explosive mixture in a closed space. Keep sparks and flames away.

questions.stem: How should a propane or welding gas cylinder be stored aboard?
options: Wedged in a closed locker with the valve open
Upright, valve shut, secured and ventilated, away from heat
Next to the engine so the gas stays warm
Lying loose in the bilge, out of the way
questions.explanation: Cylinders are secured against movement, kept upright and shut off, with ventilation so leaked gas cannot pool. Keep oil and grease off oxygen fittings.
